title: try
goal: In this lesson you will learn how a try block marks code that might fail.
learn: Indent the risky lines under try
Remember that try needs an except to go with it
idea: Sometimes a line might fail. You wrap that code in try:. Python runs the indented try block first. If something breaks, it can jump to an except block, which you will meet in the next lessons. For now just focus on putting the risky code under try:.
changeOneLine: In the editor above, change friends = 3 to friends = 0 and press Run. You should see the except message.

practice.text: Put the division inside try (keep a simple except that prints Oops). friends is 2.
practice.hint: Move print(a / b) under try: with four spaces. Add except: below it, lined up with try, and put print("Oops") inside.
practice.starterTip:
Structure: try:
    print(a / b)
except:
    print("Oops"). Delete the old print(a / b) that sits outside try.
practice.starter:
a = 10
b = 2
# try / except
print(a / b)
practice.gradingNote: Pass if try wraps the division and result prints (except unused).

practice.text: Try to int() the text '7'. Print the number inside try.
practice.hint: Under try:, convert text with int(text) and then print it. Indent both lines with four spaces.
practice.starterTip: Inside the blank under try:, add: n = int(text) and print(n). You should see 7.
practice.gradingNote: Pass if 7 prints from inside try using int.

quiz.question: What does try: mark?
quiz.correct: Right, try wraps the risky lines.
quiz.wrong: Put the shaky code under try.

quiz.question: Must try code be indented?
quiz.correct: Yes, blocks in Python are indented.

quiz.question: If try succeeds, what happens to except?
quiz.correct: Right, except only runs when try fails.
quiz.wrong: On the success path, except is skipped.
